newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: ALPINE SKIING-WIBERG KEEPS COMPOSURE FOR FOURTH WIN.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-WIBERG KEEPS COMPOSURE FOR FOURTH WIN.

text.p: Pernilla Wiberg, a picture of composure through a chaotic three days at this Austrian resort, recorded her fourth World Cup victory of the season in a Super-G on Sunday.
The 26-year-old Swede postest the fastest time of one minute 39.98 seconds on a hard, icy 2,000-metre long course, ahead of Italian world super-G champion Isolde Kostner, who clocked 1:40.26.
"The weather was perfect today. The slope was hardened by the cold overnight temperatures. It was icy and that's just the way I like it," said Wiberg, a triple world and twice Olympic champion.
Wiberg remained unaffected by the heavy fog, snow and poor visibility which led to a downhill being called off on Friday and moved forward by a day.
Organisers then scheduled two downhills for Saturday, of which only one could be carried out because of similar bad weather conditions on the Strohsack piste.
Wiberg, who is still chasing a maiden downhill triumph, finished an excellent fifth in that race, which was won by Swiss veteran Heidi Zurbriggen.
Sunday's victory, Wiberg's second in super-G this winter after winning in Lake Louise, Canada, in November increased her leading total in the overall standings to 863 points.
She is now 214 points ahead of her fiercest rival, titleholder Katja Seizinger of Germany, who was third on Sunday in 1:40.34.

"My goal this winter is to win the World Cup titles in downhill and slalom," said Wiberg, formerly a technical specialist who has recently become a formidable all-rounder capable of top placings in all five alpine events.
She currently heads the super-g standings with 309 points, ahead of Germany's Hilde Gerg (280), and the slalom standings in which she has 410 points.
This winter, Wiberg has also won slaloms in Semmering, Austria, and Maribor, Slovenia.

"To perform well in all disciplines you have to train well and convince yourself in your mind that you can do it," said Wiberg. "Then it's no problem. I am also convinced I can retain my good form throughout the whole season."
Although Wiberg has had her sights firmly set on the coveted overall title for the past years, she has lately refused to comment on the subject.
Her new coach, Italian Heinz-Peter Platter, said Wiberg was concentrating on triumphs in separate World Cup disciplines and taking each race at a time, because this inevitably led to overall victory.

"Wiberg is an incredible athlete. Similar to (Norway's Kjetil Andre) Aamodt and (Luxembourg's Marc) Girardelli on the men's circuit," he said. "Her only weakness is that often she just wants too much."
The Norkopping native, who resides in Monaco, will also bid for downhill and slalom medals at the world championships in Sestriere, Italy, in February.

"I will probably start in all races in Sestriere. If I leave a race out then it will be the giant slalom, because I haven't been that good in giant this winter," said Wiberg, who took giant slalom gold in her first appearance at world championships in 1991.
Seizinger, a 1993 world super-G and 1994 Olympic downhill champion, was content with her performance.
"Today, I managed to avoid the huge mistakes I made in yesterday's downhill. What occurred in the downhill was bad luck but that's part of the game.
"There are still a lot of races to go and a lot can happen. I haven't given up yet," Seizinger said..
The women's circuit will resume in the German resort of Zwiesel from January 17 to 19 with two giant slaloms and slalom.
